questions.question: Explain the inheritance structure of the quadrilateral family tree and how it powers both property questions and minimum-test proofs.
questions.expected_answer: Each generation keeps everything inherited and adds one property: parallelogram (opposite sides parallel and equal, opposite angles equal, diagonals bisect each other), rectangle adds right angles (forcing equal diagonals), rhombus adds equal sides (forcing perpendicular, angle-bisecting diagonals), and the square inherits from both. Downwards, a square's properties are the accumulated lists. Upwards, prove only the cheapest ticket — diagonals bisecting each other for a parallelogram, one right angle or equal diagonals to upgrade to rectangle, adjacent equal sides for rhombus — and inheritance supplies the rest.

questions.question: Using A(1; 3) and B(6; 15), state the three coordinate formulas and the parallel and perpendicular gradient relationships.
questions.expected_answer: Distance: root of the x-difference squared plus the y-difference squared — root of 25 + 144 = 13 (Pythagoras with the differences as legs). Midpoint: average each coordinate — (3,5; 9). Gradient: change in y over change in x — 12/5. Parallel lines share equal gradients; perpendicular gradients multiply to −1, so the partner of 12/5 is −5/12 (flip and negate).

questions.question: State the addition rule for probability and show it on the class of 36 (hockey 22, tennis 15, both 9), including the Venn filling order and the total check.
questions.expected_answer: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B): subtract the overlap once because addition counted it twice. Count: 22 + 15 − 9 = 28 play hockey or tennis, so 8 play neither. Fill the Venn overlap first (9), then hockey-only 13 and tennis-only 6, letting the outside catch the remaining 8. Check: 9 + 13 + 6 + 8 = 36, the class size — a total exceeding 36 exposes double counting.
